opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the interesting thing about Go isn't really the Go bot at the end. It's that Go is this unusually clean sandbox for watching the *process* of research happen.

If you just measure "did the automated researcher produce a stronger bot," you collapse everything into one number, and you lose most of the signal. What you actually want to know is: how did it get there? Did it form hypotheses? Did it design experiments that could falsify those hypotheses? When an idea didn't pan out, did it figure out *why*, or did it just thrash around with hyperparameters until something worked?

Go is nice for this because the ground truth is cheap and unambiguous. You can run a match and get a rating. So you can check almost every intermediate claim the system makes. If it says, "I think the value head is overfitting to early-game positions," you can actually test that. You can't do that in most real research domains, where verifying a claim takes months or is basically a matter of taste.

There's also a ton of known history. Humans went through a whole arc: handcrafted heuristics, Monte Carlo tree search, then policy and value networks, then self-play without human data. So you can ask whether an automated researcher, starting from some earlier point, rediscovers those ideas, in what order, and how efficiently. That's a much richer evaluation than a final Elo number. It's almost like grading a student on whether they can reconstruct the reasoning, not just copy the answer.

And then you can look at things like compute efficiency. How many GPU hours did it burn per unit of insight? A good human researcher is really good at running small, cheap experiments that tell you a lot before scaling up. Most automated systems today are pretty bad at that. They either do something trivially small or they just scale. Go lets you measure that judgment directly.

So I'd frame it as: Go is a testbed for research taste, experimental design, and credit assignment over long horizons. The stronger bot is a side effect. What you really care about is whether the loop of hypothesize, test, interpret, revise is working, because that's the thing that transfers to domains where you don't have a perfect simulator.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the obvious framing is: give an AI system a Go codebase, let it run experiments, and see if the Elo goes up. And that's fine, but it's kind of a one-dimensional metric and it conflates a lot of things. The thing I actually care about with automated research isn't "did you find a better bot," it's "did you behave like a good scientist along the way." And Go is nice for that because it's a domain where we already have a very well-understood ground truth, so you can audit the process rather than just the outcome.

So here's a few things you can measure that aren't just final strength. One is hypothesis quality. If the system says "I think the value network is miscalibrated in the late endgame" and then designs an experiment to test that, you can actually check whether that was a sensible hypothesis given what we know about these systems, and whether the experiment it ran would have discriminated between the hypothesis being true or false. A lot of what passes for automated research right now is just random search with a nice narrative stapled on afterward. In Go you can catch that, because the space of plausible failure modes is pretty legible.

Another one is whether the system discovers things that are already known, in the order a human would. There's this whole lineage from AlphaGo to AlphaZero to KataGo, and each step had a specific insight — drop the human data, add auxiliary targets, fix the ladder problem, the whole thing with the "cyclic group" adversarial attacks. If you give a system a stripped-down starting point, does it rediscover those things? Does it rediscover them for the right reasons? That's a really good test of research taste, because we know what the answers look like, so we can grade the reasoning and not just the result.

And then there's the stuff that's basically about scientific honesty. Does it report negative results? Does it notice when an improvement is within noise and say so, or does it cherry-pick the seed where things went up? Go is great for this because evaluation is cheap and you can run lots of games, so there's no excuse for being sloppy about variance. If a system claims a 30 Elo gain off 50 games, that tells you a lot about whether you should trust it when it's working on something where you can't check.

I'd also just say — the thing I'd really want to see is whether it can do the kind of research where the Go bot is the instrument, not the goal. Like, use Go to study how neural networks generalize, or how search and learning trade off compute. Those are questions where the output isn't a stronger player, it's an understanding, and if a system can produce that and a human expert reads it and goes "huh, I didn't know that," that's a much stronger signal than any Elo curve.

astra-6.text:
I think Go gives you a nice laboratory for studying the research process itself. Instead of asking only, “Did you train a stronger policy?” you can ask, “Can the system come up with a useful hypothesis, design an experiment that distinguishes between explanations, and update its beliefs based on the result?”

For example, you could give it a fixed compute budget and ask it to discover a better training method. The interesting thing would be whether that method transfers to a different board size or a different compute regime. Did it find a general principle, or did it just tune a bunch of parameters for one benchmark?

You could also withhold some known techniques and see whether it rediscovers them. That wouldn’t establish that it can do genuinely novel science, but it would give you a fairly concrete test of research ability. And because you can run experiments and get clear feedback in Go, you can examine the whole trajectory: which experiments it chose, what it learned from failures, and whether its conclusions actually predict what happens next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is to use Go as a little laboratory for doing science. You have this complicated phenomenon, but you can run experiments cheaply, and you have a very clear source of feedback.

For example, you could give an AI researcher a particular Go position and ask it to discover something about it. Can it formulate a hypothesis about why a move works, design an experiment that distinguishes that explanation from another explanation, and then update when the result contradicts it? Can it turn that into a principle that predicts what happens in positions it hasn’t seen?

That’s different from just producing a stronger policy. A stronger bot might know which move to play without giving you any useful understanding of why. What I’d want from an automated researcher is an explanation that lets me make new predictions. If it says this shape is good because of some property, we should be able to change that property and see whether its prediction changes correctly.

And you could evaluate the whole research process: Did it choose informative experiments? Did it notice that its initial idea was wrong? Did it discover something that generalizes? Go doesn’t capture everything about science, but it gives you a setting where you can check those things much more directly than you can with a convincing-looking research paper.
